title: Stability and Frequency Compensation
intro: Feedback only helps if the loop stays stable. Every gain stage adds a pole, and enough phase shift turns negative feedback into positive feedback. This chapter shows how to judge stability from the loop gain and how to reshape an op amp's response so the loop is well behaved (Razavi, Chapter 10).

blocks.text: For a loop with constant feedback factor $\beta$, the closed-loop response is $H/(1 + \beta H)$. If at some frequency $\beta H(j\omega_1) = -1$, the denominator vanishes and the circuit can sustain or grow an oscillation at $\omega_1$. Stability therefore depends only on the loop transmission $\beta H(s)$, and the design goal is that $|\beta H|$ falls below one well before its phase reaches $-180^{\circ}$.

Two remedies exist: reduce the phase shift (fewer poles in the signal path, which means fewer stages and less gain or swing), or make the gain fall sooner (compensation), which keeps the DC gain and swing but sacrifices bandwidth. In practice one designs for few poles first, then compensates.

blocks.alt: Two stacked Bode plots of a loop gain with two poles. The top plot shows the magnitude falling from 60 dB, crossing 0 dB near 1 MHz. The bottom plot shows the phase falling toward minus 180 degrees. A vertical dotted line links the 0 dB crossing to the phase curve, and an arrow marks the phase margin, the gap between the phase at that frequency and minus 180 degrees, about 55 degrees.
blocks.caption: Phase margin is read at the gain crossover: the distance of $\angle\beta H$ from $-180^{\circ}$.

items: Stability and Phase Margin: Barkhausen's conditions, gain and phase crossover, one-, two- and three-pole loops, root locus, how much phase margin is enough.

Frequency Compensation: compensating one-stage op amps by moving the dominant pole, why fully differential stages need little compensation, Miller compensation and pole splitting in two-stage op amps, the right-half-plane zero and the nulling resistor.
Slewing in Two-Stage Op Amps: the $I_{SS}/C_C$ slew rate and the conditions on the output stage.
Other Compensation Techniques: source-follower, common-gate (current-buffer) and cascode compensation.
Nyquist's Stability Criterion: polar plots, Cauchy's principle of the argument, systems with poles at the origin and with several $-180^{\circ}$ crossings.

blocks.text: The worst case for stability is unity-gain feedback, $\beta = 1$: lowering $\beta$ shifts $|\beta H|$ down and moves the gain crossover to lower frequency while the phase curve stays put. A loop that is stable as a buffer is stable at any higher closed-loop gain (for frequency-independent $\beta$).

blocks.text: An op amp with a dominant pole at the origin (for practical purposes) is used as a unity-gain buffer with unity-gain frequency 200 MHz. Where must its second pole be for 60° phase margin?
